characterized_levers.name: Technical Feasibility Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Demonstrating technical feasibility impacts policy. Immediate: Demonstrators built → Systemic: 15% increased policy traction due to concrete evidence → Strategic: Enhanced credibility in procurement negotiations.
options: Focus demonstrator efforts on a single, highly secure authentication method, such as FIDO2, on a mainstream Android device.
Develop demonstrators for both FIDO2 on GrapheneOS and a browser-based fallback, accepting slightly longer development timelines.
Explore passwordless authentication via blockchain-anchored identity and decentralized identifiers (DIDs) alongside FIDO2 and browser-based fallback demonstrators.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Technical Risk vs. Scope. Weakness: The options don't explicitly address the cost implications of each demonstrator approach.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on demonstrating technical feasibility to impact policy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of the technical demonstrators on policy traction, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to demonstrator development.
characterized_levers.description: This lever controls the technical demonstration strategy for proving platform-neutral authentication feasibility. It encompasses building non-production demonstrators using standards like FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect on privacy-respecting platforms, plus fallback authentication paths independent of iOS/Android app stores. Success metrics include delivering credible technical evidence that secure, standards-based access models work without exclusive reliance on Apple or Google as trust anchors, while maintaining lean, defensible scope.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Directly enables Policy Advocacy Strategy and Procurement Influence Strategy by providing concrete technical evidence that makes platform-neutral requirements defensible in procurement documents. Strong synergy with Coalition Building Strategy, as demonstrators serve as tangible proof points that strengthen coalition credibility when engaging stakeholders and policymakers.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Tension exists with Procurement Influence Strategy regarding timeline: extensive technical demonstration work (phase two, months 9–16) delays policy intervention, while procurement windows may close before demonstrators are mature. Also conflicts with rapid Coalition Building Strategy if development timelines stretch, reducing momentum for early political engagement during critical phase-one advocacy window.

characterized_levers.name: Policy Advocacy Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Policy advocacy shapes procurement. Immediate: Policy proposals submitted → Systemic: 20% greater likelihood of influencing AltID requirements → Strategic: Increased adoption of platform-neutral standards.
options: Focus advocacy on continuity of service and supplier concentration risks, avoiding direct privacy arguments.
Balance continuity arguments with privacy and democratic accountability concerns, broadening the coalition.
Prioritize open-source governance and community-led development models for digital identity, framing platform neutrality as a public good.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Political Risk vs. Coalition Size. Weakness: The options don't consider the potential for regulatory capture by incumbent vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on policy advocacy shaping procurement, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of policy advocacy on influencing AltID requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to advocacy focus.
characterized_levers.description: This lever shapes the narrative and messaging strategy for influencing policy and procurement decisions. It involves reframing digital identity resilience as a public-sector risk, emphasizing supplier concentration, continuity of service, and procurement neutrality, while selectively incorporating privacy and democratic accountability arguments. Success is measured by formal institutional responses from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and inclusion of platform-neutrality language in AltID-related procurement or policy documents.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Amplifies Coalition Building Strategy by crafting messages that resonate across diverse stakeholder groups—security experts, privacy advocates, civil society, and procurement officials. Strong synergy with EU Standards Engagement Strategy, as resilience-focused framing aligns with broader European interoperability and portability objectives, making Danish advocacy easier to integrate into EU-level discussions.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Conflicts with Technical Feasibility Strategy on prioritization: focusing advocacy on continuity and supplier risk messaging may demand policy submissions before demonstrators are complete, forcing premature claims about feasibility. Also tensions with Coalition Building Strategy if messaging alienates incumbent operators or prioritizes continuity over privacy, potentially narrowing civil-society support.

characterized_levers.name: Coalition Building Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Coalition strength amplifies advocacy. Immediate: Stakeholder engagement increased → Systemic: 30% stronger advocacy position in procurement discussions → Strategic: Greater political pressure for platform neutrality.
options: Build a narrow coalition focused on security experts and contingency-planning stakeholders.
Expand the coalition to include civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers.
Actively recruit dissenting voices from within the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen to foster internal debate.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Speed vs. Breadth of Support. Weakness: The options fail to address the potential for conflicting priorities within the coalition.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on coalition building to amplify advocacy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of coalition strength on advocacy position, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to coalition composition.
characterized_levers.description: This lever orchestrates stakeholder engagement across civil society, academia, security experts, privacy advocates, and sympathetic policymakers to build political pressure for platform-neutral digital identity. The coalition amplifies advocacy reach and credibility during procurement and standards processes. Success metrics include documented stakeholder matrix, lead times, decision gates, and sufficient coalition breadth to sustain advocacy pressure through phases two and three.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Directly strengthens Policy Advocacy Strategy by expanding the audience and legitimacy of platform-neutrality messages, making institutional resistance harder. Powerful synergy with Procurement Influence Strategy: a broad, visible coalition of credible voices (academics, civil society, security experts) creates political cost for procurement officials who ignore platform-neutral requirements.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Inherent tension with Procurement Influence Strategy if coalition includes conflicting priorities—privacy advocates may demand stronger open-source governance while procurement officials prioritize rapid deployment. Also conflicts with Technical Feasibility Strategy if coalition pressures for immediate policy action before demonstrators mature, forcing overstatement of technical readiness.

characterized_levers.name: Procurement Influence Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Procurement influence drives adoption. Immediate: Platform-neutral language included in procurement documents → Systemic: 25% faster scaling through mandated supplier diversity → Strategic: Reduced long-term dependency on Apple and Google.
options: Focus on including general language about supplier concentration risk in AltID procurement documents.
Advocate for specific requirements for platform-neutral access and certified fallback authentication paths.
Propose a 'digital sovereignty bonus' in procurement scoring, rewarding vendors who demonstrably reduce platform dependency.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Specificity vs. Implementability. Weakness: The options don't account for the potential for vendors to game the procurement process.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on procurement influence driving adoption, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of procurement influence on scaling, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to procurement language.
characterized_levers.description: This lever controls the intervention mechanism for embedding platform-neutrality and fallback-access requirements into AltID and related digital identity procurement documents and standards. It involves crafting specific language around supplier concentration risk, fallback authentication paths, and platform independence, then inserting that language into official design, policy, or procurement processes. Success is measured by actual inclusion of such requirements in at least one AltID-related document.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Directly leverages Technical Feasibility Strategy demonstrators as evidence that requirements are achievable, reducing procurement push-back. Synergizes strongly with Coalition Building Strategy: a visible, credible coalition creates political pressure that makes procurement officials more receptive to platform-neutral language, even when incumbent vendors object.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Fundamental conflict with Policy Advocacy Strategy timing: broad advocacy campaigns may alert incumbent vendors early, triggering lobbying and regulatory capture before procurement windows open. Also tension with EU Standards Engagement Strategy if Danish procurement moves faster than EU harmonization, creating inconsistency or forcing rework later.

characterized_levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: EU standards engagement creates broader impact. Immediate: Input provided to relevant EU bodies → Systemic: 10% increased alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements → Strategic: Enhanced interoperability and reduced lock-in across Europe.
options: Monitor relevant EU bodies and technical working groups, providing occasional input on interoperability.
Actively engage with EU bodies, advocating for platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms in eIDAS2 and related standards.
Champion a 'sovereign identity sandbox' within the EU Digital Identity Wallet framework to test and validate platform-neutral authentication models.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Resource Allocation vs. Scope of Influence. Weakness: The options don't address the potential for EU standards to be influenced by large platform vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on EU standards engagement creating broader impact, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of EU standards engagement on alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to EU engagement strategies.
characterized_levers.description: This lever orchestrates engagement with European Digital Identity Wallet bodies, eIDAS2 working groups, and relevant EU technical standards forums. It aims to embed platform-neutral access, interoperability, and certified fallback mechanisms into European standards and wallet specifications, creating broader structural pressure for reduced platform lock-in across EU member states. Success metrics include documented input to at least one official EU body and alignment of European standards language with Danish platform-neutrality objectives.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Amplifies Policy Advocacy Strategy by aligning Danish advocacy with broader European requirements, making domestic resilience arguments part of a larger EU-level consensus on interoperability and portability. Synergizes with Procurement Influence Strategy by creating EU-level standards pressure that makes Danish procurement officials' platform-neutral choices appear aligned with European direction rather than exceptional.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Tension with Procurement Influence Strategy on timeline: EU standards processes are slow; Danish procurement decisions may be locked in before EU standards mature, forcing Denmark to lead unilaterally or abandon platform-neutrality language. Also conflicts with Coalition Building Strategy if EU-level work diverts resources from domestic coalition maintenance, reducing domestic political pressure during critical procurement windows.
